analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $7.25 and ties future raises to congressional pay increases.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2006 with 13 cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote and died when Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in three steps — to $5.85, then $6.55, then $7.25 an hour — up from the $5.15 level in place since 1997 [S2][S3]. It also contained an unusual enforcement mechanism: every year after that, the minimum wage would automatically rise by the same percentage as the annual pay increase Members of Congress give themselves [S2][S3]. The idea was that if lawmakers' pay goes up, minimum-wage workers' pay should too. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers earning the federal minimum wage of $5.15 an hour would have seen raises totaling $2.10 an hour over roughly two years, to $7.25 [S2][S3]. After that, their wage would rise automatically whenever congressional pay rose, protecting it from being frozen for years at a time as it had been since 1997 [S2][S3]. Workers paid just above the minimum could also benefit as pay scales shifted upward.

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.85 an hour 60 days after enactment, to $6.55 a year later, and to $7.25 two years later [S2][S3].

After the initial increases, the minimum wage automatically rises each year by the same percentage as the annual pay adjustment for Members of Congress, so it can no longer sit unchanged for a decade as it did after the 1997 increase [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage labor — restaurants, retail stores, and other businesses that pay at or near the minimum — would bear the higher payroll cost, and some would likely pass part of it to customers through higher prices. Millions of minimum-wage workers would gain roughly $4,000 a year at full implementation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: Businesses that employ large numbers of minimum-wage workers would face higher labor costs, and small businesses in low-wage sectors argued such increases force price hikes, reduced hours, or fewer entry-level jobs; this is the standard and genuine trade-off of any minimum-wage increase.

Tying the minimum wage to congressional pay raises is an unusual mechanism: it delegates wage policy to whatever Congress decides to pay itself, and if Members' pay were frozen, the minimum wage would stay frozen too — replacing one political bottleneck with another.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers affected, the benefit is direct and substantial: a raise from $5.15 to $7.25 an hour is a 41% increase for people at the bottom of the pay scale. The costs fall on employers of low-wage labor, some of which would raise prices or trim hours. The indexing-to-congressional-pay design is clever politics but imperfect policy, since it makes the minimum wage hostage to Congress's own pay decisions. On balance, this was a straightforward wage increase whose main design flaw was political symbolism rather than economics.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2006 and referred to the Senate labor committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Hillary Clinton introduced the bill on May 4, 2006, joined as original cosponsors by Senators Kennedy, Jeffords, Leahy, Harkin, and Obama [S3].
Thirteen senators cosponsored the bill — 12 Democrats and 1 Independent; no Republican cosponsored it [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on May 4, 2006, the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no committee markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses paying the $5.15 minimum wage kept the status quo, since the bill died without ever reaching a committee or floor vote. Minimum-wage workers gained nothing from this bill, though Congress passed a minimum wage increase in the next Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced far enough to produce a recorded vote.

industries.note: Food service is the largest employer of minimum-wage workers, so a 41% wage floor increase would have directly raised its labor costs; the industry generally opposes federal minimum wage increases. Its gain from the bill dying was keeping the $5.15 wage.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Retailers and similar businesses paying at or near the minimum would have absorbed higher payroll costs and likely passed some on through prices. Keeping the wage frozen spared them that cost.
Workers at or near the $5.15 minimum would have gained up to $2.10 an hour, roughly $4,000 a year at full implementation, plus automatic future increases tied to congressional pay.
